paras: Auburn lay 2.5 on the road. Mississippi State are without Kamario Taylor, who started six games, threw for 1448 yards and 17 touchdowns at a 71.2 grade, and has not appeared since October 17. He is not on this morning's depth chart. AJ Swann has the first-team job.

That loss is severe and it is already in the recent numbers. Mississippi State scored 62, 38, 41, 31 and 23 in Taylor's five healthy starts and 15, 3 and 23 in the three games since, which is 39.0 a game against 13.7. Their season average of 26.2 describes neither team.

The pick survives because Auburn have fallen further over the same stretch. They have scored 19.3 a game across their last three and allowed 35.3, their coverage grades 60.2 and ranks 125th of 138, and they are 2-7 against the spread, 131st. Run on each side's last three games the points check has Mississippi State winning by 4.2, which is wider than the 2.8 the full-season version gives. Taking a team whose quarterback is out needs the opponent to be worse, and here the numbers say Auburn are.

Syracuse lay three on the road. SP+ separates these teams by 0.4 of a point before home field, and once home field is applied the rating has NC State winning by 2.7. The points check agrees on the side at 1.0.

Syracuse's passing game grades 59.7, which is 114th of 138, and their offence overall is 101st. NC State score 28.9 a game to Syracuse's 29.3, so the scoring is level while the throwing is not. A road favourite whose passing ranks in the bottom twenty-five is being asked to win by more than a field goal.

NC State are 3-6 against the spread, 112th, and their defence ranks 107th in Finishing Drives, so Syracuse will move the ball. The number is the argument here rather than the matchup: three points between two 4-5 teams the ratings cannot separate, with the home side getting them.

Fresno State rank 6th in Explosiveness and 12th in Field Position, which is the counterweight.

The role is settled and it is the reason the production holds. Sixty-nine targets in nine games is 7.7 a game, and at a 9.1 average depth of target he is a volume receiver rather than a deep threat. TCU's defence is the problem: 91.8 overall and 15th nationally, with 15.8 points allowed a game. The game total is 44.5, the lowest on these picks. A 29.5 line survives a low-scoring game better than a high one does, because it needs three catches rather than a performance, but this is the pick most exposed to the opponent.
